title: Empty minds, full bellies
hookLine: don't prize the clever, and people won't compete (Tao Te Ching 3)

cards: On Monday the office starts a step challenge, with a leaderboard on the kitchen wall. By Wednesday people are pacing during phone calls.

By Friday someone is walking laps of the parking lot at nine at night, and two old friends have stopped eating lunch together because one of them is, frankly, cheating. Nobody set out to make enemies.
A board went up, and a contest grew out of it. Chapter three of the Tao Te Ching has a short, sharp idea about where contests come from.

teach.b: First, what you prize, people chase. Legge's translation opens: "Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to keep the people from rivalry among themselves."
Put a crown on cleverness, and everyone competes for the crown. The contest comes from the prize.
Second, rare things make thieves. Don't treasure things that are hard to get, the chapter says, and people won't steal; don't parade what stirs up wanting, and minds stay settled.
A rare sneaker, a hard-to-get ticket: the rarity is what makes people grab.
Third, empty minds, full bellies. The sage, the chapter says, empties people's minds and fills their bellies, softens their ambitions and strengthens their bones. Readers hear this two ways.
Some hear a ruler keeping people simple and quiet, and find it uneasy reading. Others hear a life not crowded with comparison: fed, sturdy, and not hungry for rank.

teach.h: TAKE THE PRIZE OFF THE WALL.
teach.b: The Chinese word here for mind also means heart, and some readers take the emptying as an emptying of wanting more than of thought. Readers still hold both views.
Fourth, no contest. When the sage acts without forcing, the chapter closes, nothing falls out of order. Take the prize off the wall, and the race has nowhere to go.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter three in different ways: some as advice to rulers, others as personal practice, noticing what they prize and letting go of contests that grow out of it.

games.q: you run the office. the step-challenge leaderboard has turned friends into rivals. what does chapter three suggest?

take the board off the wall.
games.why: chapter three goes to the source: don't prize it, and people won't compete for it. take the prize away, and the race has nowhere to go.

practice: Let your mind run over the last few days and find one scoreboard: who replied faster, who looks better, who works later.
Picture taking that board off the wall, so the race stops and the other person is just a person again, and breathe there with nothing to win.
If you pray, you can set the contest down in prayer; if not, let your shoulders drop as the race ends.

wordCard.voice: Empty minds. In chapter three, minds emptied of wanting and comparing, alongside full bellies and strong bones. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, xū qí xīn: empty their minds. Xīn means both heart and mind.

carryVoice: Your line: no contest. With the prize off the wall, the other runner is just a neighbor again. Same time tomorrow.
